messages.body_plain:
I just looked over the final design in looking to doc it and unfortunately
just caught a major issue, one that's bad enough I think we should fix before
releasing.  We absolutely are not going to release this now and then change
it later.  So if people really want it this way ASAP, we'll have to stick to the
broken design.

Here's what the doc says in csr_matrix_times_vector.hpp

     *  A compressed Sparse Row (CSR) sparse matrix is defined by four
     *  component vectors labeled w, v, u, and z.  They are defined as:
     *    - w: the non-zero values in the sparse matrix.
     *    - v: column index for each value in w,  as a result this
     *      is the same length as w.
     *    - u: index of where each row starts in w,  length
     *      is equal to the number of rows plus one.  Last entry is
     *      one-past-the-end in w, following the Eigen spec.
     *    - z: number of non-zero entries in each row of w,  length is
     *      equal to the number of rows.

Issue 1:  We only need one of u or v!  You can compute one from the other
directly and there's no reason to pass both of them around.  If you
look on the Wikipedia page, you see only the u array, not the z array.
At the very least, if you don't like the algorithm-internal index fiddling,
you could pay the cost and compute z inside.

  vector<int> u_to_z(const vector<int>& u) {
    vector<int> z(u.size() + 1);
    z[
    for (size_t i = 0; i < u.size(); ++i)
      z[i] =

  }

Issue 2:  I really don't like the names csr_extract_w, csr_extract_v,
csr_extract_u, and csr_extract_v, which are meant to map from a dense
matrix to the components of a sparse matrix.  I'd much prefer this:

  vector<double> csr_values(const Matrix<double, Dynamic, Dynamic>&);

  vector<int> csr_col_indexes(const Matrix<double, Dynamic, Dynamic>&);

  vector<int> csr_row_starts(const Matrix<double, Dynamic, Dynamic>&);

  Matrix<double, Dynamic, Dynamic> csr_to_matrix(const vector<double>& vals,
                                                 const vector<int>& col_indexes,
                                                 const vector<int>& row_starts,
                                                 int num_cols);

If nobody else has time to do this, I can just push everything else I'm working
on back and do this for a few days.  I'll have to read up on the specs and
understand all the tests if I'm going to contribute.

- Bob

The Eigen library sparse matrix format follows the four-vector definition (http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox-devel/group__TutorialSparse.html).  They do this because you _can_ calculate u from v and z from u, but _only_ if w has no garbage values.  In the Eigen spec, w is allowed to have garbage values so that it can avoid re-allocating memory when non-zero values are added to rows.

I wrote the functions this way with the idea that we're learning about how to interface Stan with Eigen's sparse format on the fly.  I guess we could try and optimise the format just for the use case we have in front of us, but as you say we're not going to want to change the interface to these sparse matrix functions in the language later.  Lacking any serious cost to the decision to store all four vectors, I'd rather stick to the Eigen spec.

For example, there are tests in the current version that are redundant at the moment (as Eigen seems to not pre-allocate any garbage values when going dense-to-sparse by default, currently) but they should tell us if such a change breaks any of the extractors.  At the moment the multiplication function also does not rely on a contiguous ''w''.

Another positive aspect of just monkeying Eigen as I did is that most of the code I wrote is a thin wrapper around Eigen functions.  If Eigen changes from version to version how much they use garbage values in 'w' all this code should still run fine and all the tests will still be consistent  (well, extract_z will break because it relies on the connection you noticed but that's a quick fix).  Personally I'd really like to stay clear of trying to figure out Eigen's SparseMatrix memory management as I dig further into how to use sparse matrices in Stan.

I think this means I can see where you're coming from but I still disagree with the changes you are making.

OK.  I'll leave it as is.  Thanks for explaining.

I'm not able to write the LaTeX doc until I understand
these "garbage" values and how they play into the interface.
I didn't see any explanation in the Doxygen doc for the function.
So if supporting "garbage" values is critical, then we need

* the doxygen doc for how "garbage" values work  --- the point
  is that the doc should be a contract for how the function works.

  And we should point out we're using something like an "augmented"
  CSR, not the one you'll find in the Wikipedia --- a pointer to
  Eigen's doc is OK because we depend on Eigen

* test cases to make sure the "garbage" values work as documented

If you can do the doxygen doc, I can translate to LaTeX doc very easily.

I think it's critical to do the testing before we merge.   We've been bitten
by too many loosely tested functions before.

Sorry I didn't catch the naming the first time around.  Going forward,
I would very very much prefer names with meaning rather than symbols,
letters, or numbers.  For what it's worth, I dislike "neg_binomial_2" for
the same reason as "csr_extract_w".  But at some point, we have to trade
clarity for brevity.  I can live with them like this.

I don't remember even seeing conversion functions (not that I'd bet
the farm I didn't see them) and didn't notice the redundancy in the
basic function or I'd have said something the first time around.  I think
we're going to need to put some process in for functional specs that
can be reviewed.  And by functional specs, I just mean the function signatures
and definitions.  Basically what the doxygen doc looks like.
As soon as I looked at the doxygen doc the redundancy and non-semantic function
names jumped out at me.

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

The case of having only very few observed states is not so special. Indeed it is the most common one and with the current design Stan cannot solve a large class of problems where it would be very interesting to use. The reason is that oftentimes literature knowledge is available whenever you can write down a large ODE system. The presentation from Thierry shows such a case:

http://page-meeting.org/pdf_assets/5612-PAGE2015_TW.pdf

He had to use Nonmem for his problem which includes N=16 ODE equations and M=15 parameters. So Stan currently calculates 512 ODEs, but since only one compartment is observed you only need to calculate 47! So a reduction in the size of the ODE system by a factor of >10 which is a huge speedup. Ok, this may be an extreme example, but many real-world problems are like this, i.e. many compartments are never observed, they are just created to model a physical process.

Frederic may confirm this case and relevance for practical applications, I guess.

To solve this problem would need to somehow tell the integrate_ode function which sensitivities to track from which compartment - if it is ok to let users specify that, then this appears to me easily to be addressed. The utility would be immense.

Concerning (stiff) ODE solvers: What Stan urgently needs is just a different ODE solver than the boost one! I.e. the cvode non-stiff solver runs very fast on problems where the boost solver just freezes. I suppose other non-stiff solvers (which don't increase precision indefinetly on a bad luck draw like the boost one) will do as well a good job.

Sebastian

@ Michael: If you have some math written up concerning NUTS and ODEs, I would appreciate a copy of that

messages.subject: Lingering ODE Questions
messages.body_plain:
I put together a test for the ODE sensitivities and the good news
is that our current implementation is correct.   The bad news is
that I have no idea why.  And there are some additional questions.

a) The logical discrepancy is in the sensitivities for the initial
conditions.  According to the derivation in the attached pdf
(and some experiments on analytic systems) those sensitivities
need to be incremented by one when transforming from the
shifted to the unshifted system, but I can’t find where this is
done in the code!

b) To get integrate_ode to work I need to include the (seemingly
unnecessary files)

#include <stan/math/prim/mat/meta/get.hpp>
#include <stan/math/prim/arr/meta/get.hpp>
#include <stan/math/prim/mat/meta/length.hpp>
#include <stan/math/prim/arr/meta/length.hpp>
#include <stan/math/rev/scal/fun/value_of_rec.hpp>

These seem to be related to various checks — but
why do they have to be included at this high level?

c) The sensitivities coming out of integraet_ode
are _really_ inaccurate.  I wonder how much error
the nominal integrator settings are admitting
into hard problems and how much this might be
affecting performance.  In any case we really
should expose an integrate_ode function with
customizable tolerances.

All Stan needs to do is hand over control over output by relying on callbacks.  I could see two ways of doing it:

1) Create a Stan interface that relies on streaming everything (model, data, etc...) through protocol buffers (?) and provide the necessary callbacks as part of that interface. I'm not saying either option is straightforward but with the current refactor I don't think it's outlandish either.

messages.subject: The future of stan-users
messages.body_plain:
We’ve talked a bit recently about converting stan-users to more of a forum / message board than the current mailing list format. I think this is inevitable at some point (if the user base keeps growing then we’re going to outgrow the mailing list format), but I’d like to propose that we consider making the switch sooner rather than later (especially with the rstanarm package soon to make a public appearance but also because I think stan-users is not a particularly user-friendly or dev-friendly experience).

The advantages of the message board are many, but I think the biggest gain would be the ability to have forums for each interface, one for Stan language/syntax, one for more theoretical questions, etc. This would be more organized, easier for users to navigate (and find answers to their question so they don’t post duplicates), and I think also easier for us to navigate and find the questions we're each best suited to answer.

The only downside I can think of is that Google’s version of the message board / forum would not allow us to interact with it exclusively via email. (Daniel, am I remembering that correctly?) For some of you I assume this is a big downside.

I'm not sure if it's worth moving away from Google, but I think we're already starting to outgrow the mailing list and we should seriously consider some alternatives sooner rather than later.

Thoughts?

messages.subject: backward compatibility
messages.body_plain:
It sounds like RStan 2.8 changed the way things worked
given the rant on the user's list.  Now if this is just
an issue of some minor graphics output, I'm less concerned
than if some of the estimation functions changed signatures
in a way that's not backward compatible.

The problem is that users build up workflows based on
an existing API, so when it changes, the rug gets pulled out
from under them.

I very very much want to stick to transparent semantic versioning:

  major.minor.patch

New features get a minor++, bug fix releases patch++, and
anything that breaks backward compatiblity, major++.

That is, I don't think we should break backward compatiblity
except for major releases.  Is there a way to retrofit things
so that API alls from RStan 2.7 continue to work in 2.8?

- Bob

messages.subject: specialized ODE sensitivity solvers
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

This discussion should have started on dev. So let's move it here. For the record this is about why using a specialized ODE+sensitivity solver is a very good idea, triggered by the performance comparisons here:

http://www.biomedcentral.com/content/pdf/1752-0509-6-46.pdf

In a nutshell, the advantage of doing such an approach when one has N states and K parameters is that the naive approach solves a N*(K+1) coupled system. Hence, in stiff regions the Jacobian of this coupled system is needed which is of size N*(K+1) times N*(K+1). Now, using a specialized approach we have to solve K+1 systems independently of one another (each of size N), but with a shared Jacobian of size N times K. There are a couple of big advantages with doing this in a specialized way:

1. Each subsystem is much smaller and the Jacobian is only N times K, i.e. one automatically takes advantage of the fact that the huge coupled Jacobian is banded. So you do not need to specify the sparse (coupled) Jacobian structure if you were to solve the big thing in the naive approach; by solving the K systems independently from one another you get the sparseness for free.

2. Each subsystem is solved almost independently of the other subsystems - which means that if one sub-system is very stiff compared to the others, then only the difficult (very stiff) subsystem is handled with a particular small step-size.

3. Doing the naive approach for stiff problems requires that you come up with the Jacobian of the coupled systems - which is essentially the Hessian of the original problem and would require second-order AD. In the integrated approach, you never need the second-order derivative, but you only need the Jacobian of the original system.

4. Each sensitivity system is of the form s' = J * s + f. So it is a linearized version of the original system, this can be taken into account when solving this. I don't know how, but the CVODES guide says so.

Some comments for the performance comparisons in the paper above: I agree that they could give more precise details. To my understanding they give to all algorithms the sensitivity system in analytic form. Moreover, to make the comparison more fair between the specialized and the non-specialized (wrt to ODE sensitivities) solvers, they enabled sparse Jacobians for radau5 and for ode15s. BTW, radau5 is an implicit Runge-Kutta solver and ode15s is similar to cvode. So the ode15s curves in the paper do roughly correspond to using cvode with a sparse Jacobian structure. Clearly, using the specialized CVODES gives you a substantial performance boost in many applications. For CVODES you can rely on finite diffs or you can give to CVODES the sensitivity system in analytic form. Specifying in analytic form requires you to give CVODES a function which then calculates the sensitivities - in Stan this could either be user-specified gradients at some point or a function which uses AD to calculate things.

The paper wants to sell an even better approach than CVODES offers - and their method is certainly better when you go with the comparisons there. In any case, you see that using a specialized approach like CVODES gives you already quite a boost wrt to radau5/ode15s with sparse Jacobians. The paper writes that they also have their algorithm available as C code - I don't know the license of that one, but maybe this is also an option. This can be explored, but relying on CVODES for its known and well tested history wouldn't be a bad choice.

Cheers,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Robust RK45 ODE integrator
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Currently, the use of the ODE integrator is very limited as it may freeze easily Stan whenever a unlucky parameter is tried out which renders the ODE system too stiff to attain an accuracy as requested.

That is, odeint does not fail in these situations which is what would make the system robust. I figured that we were unlucky with the choice of the integration scheme in odeint. That is, the dense_output scheme does not have any means to protect against this situation. Now, the controlled_stepper scheme does protect against this! That is, after 1000 tries, the controlled_stepper will throw an exception which gives Stan the required robustness.

Issue: https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/179
Branch with fix for it: https://github.com/stan-dev/math/tree/feature/issue-179-robust-integrator

I tested this on a 2-cmt oral dosing system which did kill Stan in iteration 3 so far with the old scheme. Now, the integrator simply rejects a few draws at the beginning, but then Stan continues sampling.

I hope this can get in quickly... as now people do not freeze Stan anymore.

Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
value_of_rec returns the underlying double value, no matter the autodiff order (fvar<var> or fvar<fvar<var> >) whereas value_of will return the nested var or fvar.

So, value_of(fvar<var> x) returns x.val_ whereas value_of_rec(fvar<var> x) returns x.val_.val()

Rob

> On Sep 30, 2015, at 5:58 AM, Ashley Ford <ashley...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> An interesting paper,

Thanks.

> (I have only read the first third so far),

Sorry for my tendency to write in the long form!

> 2 questions.
> 1. Should an Rcpp interface to the library be reasonably straightforward ?

What do you want to do with it from R?  The point of the library
is to let you take derivatives of templated C++ programs.

> 2. on my CentOS 6.7 system g++ is rather old
> g++ (GCC) 4.4.7 20120313 (Red Hat 4.4.7-16)
> and although the simple example from the paper works, at least one test in make test-headers  fails (its 206/866) error below.

Thanks for the careful reporting.  We should've included <stdexcept> in
that file.  No idea why the header tests are passing elsewhere --- I wonder if
it's a bug in the way they are configured externally with a driver program
including things it shouldn't.  I created an issue, which I'm sure Daniel
will be able to sort out.  Here's the tracker:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/186

I'll make sure to thank you in our acknowledgements, too.

> Can I assume if my programs compile OK with this compiler they are OK or do I need to get an alternative version of gcc ?

We've had issues on and off with g++ 4.4, which seems
to be somewhat of an outlier in terms of behavior.

I would update your GCC for two reasons:  better behavior with
recent code, faster compilation, and generation of more efficient code.
Better yet, get a recent version of clang++ --- it compiles way faster
and generates code for Stan that's just as efficient at -O3 --- and we
rely heavily on compiler optimizations in Stan Math.

- Bob
